Alzheimer’s disease (AD)

Two sham-controlled trials in mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease reported short-term cognitive-test gains. A separate 20-person trial in broader MCI also found cognitive signals, but no study has established improved everyday function or slower disease progression.

Two 2021 reports describe the same 60-person trial cohort.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

MCI due to Alzheimer’s disease, confirmatory RCT (Chun et al. 2026; n=80): MoCA-K change +3.87±2.51 points with active treatment versus −0.74±2.85 with placebo over 12 weeks (p<0.001). K-MMSE2 and CERAD-K measures also favored active treatment.

MCI due to Alzheimer’s disease, RCT (Chun et al. 2025; n=26): K-MoCA improved versus sham at week 13 (p<0.05); K-MMSE2 did not differ significantly between groups. A numerical between-group K-MoCA estimate is not reported in the indexed abstract.

Broader MCI, sham-controlled pilot (Rashidi-Ranjbar et al. 2026; n=20; not AD-specific): MMSE change +1.00±1.25 active versus −0.50±1.58 sham; difference 1.50 points (95% CI 0.16–2.84; p=0.03; d=1.05). CVLT-II long-delay recognition favored active treatment (p=0.02; d=1.09).

These are short-term cognitive-test results. No clinical effect estimate for everyday function or long-term disease progression is available.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term cognitive test scores in mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease (Chun et al. 2025; Chun et al. 2026)

Low for everyday function and long-term disease progression (Chun et al. 2025; Chun et al. 2026)

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two sham-controlled trials in mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease reported short-term cognitive-test gains. A separate 20-person trial in broader MCI also found cognitive signals, but no study has established improved everyday function or slower disease progression.

Summary of the Evidence

Two sham-controlled trials in mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease reported short-term cognitive-test gains. A small sham-controlled trial in broader MCI also found cognitive signals, but did not require Alzheimer-specific criteria. No study has established improved everyday independence or slower disease progression.

Human and clinical evidence

A 26-person randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial enrolled people meeting NIA-AA criteria for MCI due to Alzheimer’s disease. Participants used home transcranial 808-nm light six days a week for 12 weeks. At week 13, K-MoCA scores improved versus sham (p<0.05); the between-group K-MMSE2 difference was not statistically significant. No serious adverse events were reported (Chun et al. 2025).

A separate confirmatory randomized, double-blind trial enrolled 80 people meeting the same MCI-due-to-Alzheimer’s criteria. Home use of 808-nm light over both dorsolateral prefrontal cortices occurred six days a week for 12 weeks. MoCA-K scores rose by 3.87±2.51 points in the active arm and fell by 0.74±2.85 in the placebo arm (p<0.001). K-MMSE2 and CERAD-K measures also favored active treatment. Depression scores did not change, and no device-related adverse events were reported (Chun et al. 2026).

A third, single-blind randomized sham-controlled pilot studied 20 adults with general MCI, without an Alzheimer-specific diagnostic requirement. A portable research device with five 810-nm LEDs was used at home for 20 minutes per session, six days a week for six weeks. MMSE improved by 1.00±1.25 points with active treatment and declined by 0.50±1.58 with sham (between-group difference 1.50; 95% CI 0.16–2.84; p=0.03; d=1.05). CVLT-II long-delay recognition also favored active treatment (p=0.02; d=1.09). This supports further MCI research but is indirect evidence for Alzheimer-specific impairment (Rashidi-Ranjbar et al. 2026).

Other human reports require narrower interpretation. Two 2021 papers report different analyses of one 60-person randomized trial in mild-to-moderate dementia; they are not independent samples, and the cohort was not uniformly diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease (Nizamutdinov et al. 2021; Qi et al. 2021). Other reports include mixed dementia populations or PBM combined with exercise, so their outcomes cannot be attributed to PBM for Alzheimer’s disease alone.

Animal evidence

Mouse, rat, and zebrafish studies examine memory, amyloid-related pathology, inflammation, and brain metabolism. Many report task or biomarker changes; one mouse study found no preventive effect. These findings do not establish patient benefit.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Cell and tissue studies examine amyloid handling, oxidative stress, mitochondrial activity, and inflammatory signaling. They help investigate possible pathways but do not test cognition or daily function in people.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The two Alzheimer-defined trials used home 808-nm near-infrared light over the forehead six days weekly for 12 weeks. The broader-MCI pilot used a portable, five-emitter, 810-nm device pulsed at 40 Hz for 20 minutes six days weekly for six weeks, targeting default-mode regions and the olfactory bulb; manufacturer and model were not reported. Other records include red and near-infrared light, helmets, intranasal devices, and combined interventions. These protocols do not establish one optimal dose or equivalence across devices.

Interpretation

Two controlled trials in MCI due to Alzheimer’s disease report short-term cognitive-test gains, with the larger confirmatory trial also favoring active treatment on additional measures. A small trial in broader MCI adds preliminary but indirect evidence. It remains unknown whether these test-score changes improve independence or alter the longer course of Alzheimer’s disease.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two independent sham-controlled trials specifically enrolling people with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease reported short-term cognitive-test improvements, including a larger 80-person confirmatory trial (Chun et al. 2025; Chun et al. 2026). A separate 20-person trial in broader MCI adds indirect evidence because it did not require Alzheimer-specific diagnostic criteria. Follow-up was short; daily function and disease progression remain untested.
